content: Pseudomonas syringae is a rod-shaped bacterium that is classified as Gram-negative and possesses polar flagella, which aid in its motility. It belongs to the genus Pseudomonas, and phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA places it within the Pseudomonas syringae group. This bacterium is a plant pathogen capable of infecting a wide variety of plant species, and it exists in the form of over 50 distinct pathovars. Historically, many of these pathovars were thought to represent separate species within the Pseudomonas genus. However, advanced molecular biology techniques, such as DNA hybridization, have confirmed that they all belong to the Pseudomonas syringae species. The bacterium derives its name from the lilac tree (Syringa vulgaris), the plant from which it was first isolated. Pseudomonas syringae is characterized by its inability to produce arginine dihydrolase and oxidase enzymes, as it tests negative for these activities. When grown on sucrose nutrient agar, it produces a polymer called levan. This bacterium secretes a lipodepsinonapeptide toxin known as syringomycin, which is harmful to plants. Additionally, when cultured on King’s B medium, it exhibits a yellow fluorescent appearance due to the production of a siderophore called pyoverdin. Notably, Pseudomonas syringae also has ice-nucleating properties, which allow it to catalyze the formation of ice crystals under certain environmental conditions. Epidemiology The development of diseases caused by Pseudomonas syringae is typically favored by wet and cool environmental conditions. The optimal temperature range for disease progression is generally between 12°C and 25°C, although this can vary depending on the specific pathovar involved. The bacterium is often seed-borne and spreads between plants primarily through rain splash. While it is a plant pathogen, Pseudomonas syringae can also survive as a saprophyte in the phyllosphere (the aerial parts of plants) when environmental conditions are not conducive to disease development. Interestingly, some saprophytic strains of Pseudomonas syringae have been utilized as biocontrol agents to combat post-harvest rots in agricultural settings. Pathovars Ribotypical analysis has led to the reclassification of several pathovars of Pseudomonas syringae into other species, such as Pseudomonas amygdali, Pseudomonas tomato, Pseudomonas coronafaciens, Pseudomonas avellanae, Pseudomonas helianthi, Pseudomonas tremae, Pseudomonas cannabina, and Pseudomonas viridiflava. The remaining pathovars of Pseudomonas syringae include the following: Pseudomonas syringae pv. aceris: Infects maple trees (Acer species). Pseudomonas syringae pv. aptata: Infects beets (Beta vulgaris). Pseudomonas syringae pv. atrofaciens: Infects wheat (Triticum aestivum). Pseudomonas syringae pv. dysoxylis: Infects the kohekohe tree (Dysoxylum spectabile). Pseudomonas syringae pv. japonica: Infects barley (Hordeum vulgare). Pseudomonas syringae pv. lapsa: Infects wheat (Triticum aestivum). Pseudomonas syringae pv. panici: Infects grass species in the Panicum genus. Pseudomonas syringae pv. papulans: Infects crabapple trees (Malus sylvestris). Pseudomonas syringae pv. pisi: Infects peas (Pisum sativum). Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae: Infects lilac (Syringa species) and beans (Phaseolus species). It is worth noting that Pseudomonas savastanoi was previously considered a pathovar or subspecies of Pseudomonas syringae. In many contexts, it is still referred to as Pseudomonas syringae pv. savastanoi. However, DNA-relatedness studies have led to its reclassification as a distinct species. Pseudomonas savastanoi itself has three host-specific pathovars: Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. fraxini, which causes ash canker. Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. nerii, which infects oleander. Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. oleae, which causes olive knot disease. Genome Sequencing Projects The genomes of several strains of Pseudomonas syringae have been sequenced. These include: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato strain DC3000. Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae strain B728a. Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola strain 1448A. Related Topics Ice-minus bacteria: Genetically modified strains of Pseudomonas syringae that lack ice-nucleating properties. Pseudomonas phage Φ6: A bacteriophage that infects Pseudomonas syringae.
